entries.summary: A device joined the fleet and is now addressable.
entries.description: Carries the device as the fleet knows it: its id, its model and the connector that admitted it. It fires once per session, when the host takes the device and registers it. A device that goes away and comes back without its session ending is carried by com.prusa.connect.device.presence.changed rather than by a second arrival, so a bouncing link does not read as a fleet of machines arriving. It is a state event rather than telemetry, because a reader that missed it holds a fleet that is missing a device.

entries.summary: A device's connection ended.
entries.description: Carries the device, the connector it arrived through and why the session ended. The record is retained: departed means unreachable, not deleted. The device stays on the listing with the last state it reported and the same reason, so a machine that was here reads differently from an id that never answered. A reader keeps the device in its list and marks it as gone, which is what stops a flapping connection emptying and refilling a screen.

entries.summary: A device became unreachable, or reachable again, without its session ending.
entries.description: Carries the device and whether it is reachable right now, so one frame states the whole answer and a reader that missed the one before it is correct again on the next. It is not a departure: the session is still open, so a command still queues for the machine and the device is still in the fleet. A link that bounces is folded into at most one frame per second per device, the last of which carries the state it settled on.

entries.summary: What this server is making of one device's frames changed.
entries.description: Carries the device and the whole link reading: whether the connector counts these at all, how many frames it had no reading of and how many telemetry patches it dropped, both as a total for the session and as a rate over the window the reading was taken across. It exists because a machine running firmware the server cannot read connects, stays connected and publishes nothing, so it looks exactly like a machine that is idle. One frame states the whole reading, and the reading is repeated while either total is moving and once more after it settles, so a reader is never left showing a storm that ended.

entries.summary: What the host has found wrong with one device changed.
entries.description: Carries the device and its whole issue list, worst first, in the shape the device listing carries, and the dialog the device is waiting on a person for, when it waits for one. A reader holding the device replaces both, and a reader that missed a frame is correct again on the next. Changes that arrive together, such as a dialog's id and its title, are folded into one frame that carries what they settled on, so a module that sends a message per frame sends one. A departure is not repeated here: the device's departure is its own event.

entries.summary: The word a device reports for what it is doing changed.
entries.description: Carries the device, the connector it arrived through, and the state before and after, as the machine spells them, such as READY and PRINTING. It fires when the value at /state differs from the one held. The first state of a device this server holds none for comes with from empty, and a device repeating the state it is in fires nothing. The same value is also published as com.prusa.connect.device.telemetry.sampled at /state; this frame exists so a reader that waits for a device to come to rest, such as a print queue, need not read every measurement of every device to find the few that change its state. It is a state event rather than telemetry, because a reader that missed it would wait for a change that already happened.

entries.summary: One measurement of a device's live state.
entries.description: Conflated and at-most-once. A slow reader is given the newest sample rather than every sample it missed, because a superseded temperature has no value and the queue it would fill does.

entries.summary: The record this server stores about one device changed.
entries.description: Carries the stored row: which connector holds the device, what the machine said it is, its firmware, whether this server holds a socket to it, why the last session ended, when it was last heard from and the tags an operator put on it. Beside them it names which of those fields moved, so a consumer acts on the change without diffing. It fires once per device per write to the record store and only when one of the named fields moved, which is why a fleet reporting telemetry at 5 Hz produces none of these: the state tree has its own frame per path and last_seen rides along here without ever causing a frame. The tree is deliberately absent, because every path in it is already published as com.prusa.connect.device.telemetry.sampled and carrying it here would store every value twice. One frame states the whole row, so a reader that missed the one before it is correct again on the next.

entries.summary: The storage devices one device reported changed.
entries.description: Carries the device and the whole list, in the shape /api/v1/devices/{device_id}/storages answers with, so one frame states the whole answer and a reader that missed the one before it is correct again on the next. It fires when an answer from the device differs from the one held, and on the first answer of each connection, which is what turns reported true. Buddy firmware reports a drive put in or pulled out on its own, and it answers when asked: on its connection, a root listing this server holds no listing for, any root listing with refresh=true, and the storages route with refresh=true.

entries.summary: A read of one device folder began or landed, or the folder changed.
entries.description: Carries the device and the folder, as the storage-prefixed path /api/v1/devices/{device_id}/files takes, and no rows. It fires when a read of the folder begins, with reading true, and when that read lands, with reading false and failed saying whether the device answered or refused, and when this server patched or forgot the folder it holds. A reader that gets it reads the folder again with refresh=false, which answers what this server holds and starts a read only when it holds nothing for the folder. Its device origin makes it visible to whoever may see the device, as com.prusa.connect.device.storages.changed is.

entries.summary: The cameras listed for one device changed.
entries.description: Carries the device and nothing else. It fires when what /api/v1/cameras?device={device_id} lists for the device changes: a camera was bound to it or taken off it, started or stopped serving, or changed its formats or its cadence. A reader that gets it reads that listing again. The cameras are not in the frame, because a camera carries grants of its own: a person may see a printer and not one of its cameras, and the listing is what applies the camera's grants. Images, live views and uploads never travel on the event stream, and neither does a value that changes with them, such as the time of the last frame: only a change to which cameras the device has or to what one can serve publishes this. A device publishes it at most once every 5 seconds. Changes inside that time are folded into one frame at its end, sent only if the list still differs from the one the last frame announced.

entries.summary: A camera was handed a new frame.
entries.description: Carries nothing but its origin, which is the camera's own device, so the camera's grants decide who gets it. It fires when a camera that is sent its pictures, such as a push camera, stores one, whether it came over HTTP or from a module. A reader that gets it loads the camera's still again instead of asking on a clock. The frame itself never travels on the stream. It is telemetry, so it is never stored, and a slow reader gets the latest one.

entries.summary: A configured instance moved between lifecycle states.
entries.description: Carries the instance's ref, its derived state and the conditions behind it. It is how a badge in a user interface changes without polling the resource API.

entries.summary: A running module changed which entries of its own interface it hides.
entries.description: Carries the instance's ref as resource, and as hidden the whole list the module hides now, each entry a slot key and an identity such as pages/customers. It is how the web app takes a page out of the sidebar, or puts it back, without a reload: it reads GET /api/v1/resources again, where the list is ui.hidden. The operator's own hidden_contributions are not in it.

entries.summary: This site's link to its parent site changed state.
entries.description: Carries the parent's address, how the parent's authorization applies on this site, the link's state and the reason for it, and the fingerprint of the key this site proves itself with. One frame states the whole reading, so a reader that missed the one before it is correct again on the next. A parent that is lost is reported here rather than in a log, because a person watching a screen is the one who has to know.

entries.summary: A person admitted one server under this site.
entries.description: Carries the link instance, the id of the server, and the person who decided, as auth_type and auth_id. The host publishes it on the route the person called, after the link confirmed the decision, so the record names the person and never the link. A module cannot publish it: every type a module emits starts with the module's own namespace. It is a state event, so a webhook and a history store receive it under the grant on the link instance and take no further one.

entries.summary: A person took away the admission of one server under this site.
entries.description: Carries the link instance, the id of the server, and the person who decided, as auth_type and auth_id. The server stays under this site with its admission marked revoked, so an operator still sees the server that was refused. It is published the same way the approval is: on the route the person called, after the link confirmed it.

entries.summary: A server this site had no record of is now under it.
entries.description: Carries the link instance, the id the server joined under, where it sits in the tree, whether this site lets it act here yet, and its public identity key. The host derives it by comparing the reading a link reports with the reading before it, so a link needs no new call and cannot report a server twice. A site that keeps every new server waiting reports the admission as pending here, and the person who then approves it is in com.prusa.connect.link.node.approved.

entries.summary: The server above refused this site's request to join.
entries.description: Carries the link instance, the address of the server above, the protocol's own number for the refusal, the link's registered code for it and the sentence the server above wrote. The two identifiers mean different things: the number is the other end's and the code is the link's, which is what a page keys its own sentence by. It is a state event rather than an audit one, because nobody on this site decided it.

entries.summary: The connection to one server under this site closed.
entries.description: Carries the link instance, the id of the server, that the connection is not open, and when something last arrived from it. The server stays under this site, so a reader marks it as gone rather than dropping it. The host derives it by comparing one reading with the reading before it, so a link that reports the same reading twice publishes nothing.

entries.summary: The connection to one server under this site opened again.
entries.description: Carries the link instance, the id of the server, that the connection is open, and when something last arrived from it. It is the answer to com.prusa.connect.link.node.lost, so a screen that marked a server as gone clears the mark on this frame rather than on the next whole reading.

entries.summary: This reader cannot be resumed from its cursor without a gap.
entries.description: The events between the reader's cursor and the stream's oldest retained position are gone. A reader that receives it refetches the state it cares about rather than assuming the gap held nothing.

entries.summary: An origin this reader followed is no longer one it may see.
entries.description: Carries the origin, as kind:id. It is sent for an origin the reader held, or named in the cursor it resumed from, and never for one it could not see. Whatever the stream had queued for that origin is dropped before it is sent. It does not say whether the origin still exists: a removed extension, a removed printer and a grant taken away read the same. A reader that named its origins explicitly is not sent it: its stream is closed instead.

entries.summary: A machine introduced itself over a connector's wire and is waiting for a decision.
entries.description: Carries the code the machine is displaying, the connector holding it, the fingerprint it keeps across reconnections, and what it said it is. The origin is the connector instance and not a device, because no device exists yet: an id is minted when the registration is approved. A page adding a printer subscribes to this instead of asking /api/v1/registrations every second. It fires once per code, when the host first writes the registration down, so a machine that retries its handshake produces one frame and not one per retry. A code a connector approves the moment it arrives is not announced, because nobody has to decide it: com.prusa.connect.device.registration.approved is its only frame. It is a state event rather than telemetry, because a reader that missed it is waiting for a code that has already arrived.

entries.summary: A registration was let through, and the machine behind it now has a device id.
entries.description: Carries the code, the connector, the fingerprint and the device id the approval bound the machine to, so a page that approved a code opens the device page from this frame alone. The device id is empty for a registration carrying no fingerprint, because there is nothing to bind an id to and the machine is given one at its first handshake. It is published for an operator's approval and for a connector configured to approve on arrival alike. Approving does not open a connection: the machine appears on /api/v1/devices once it has dialled, which is com.prusa.connect.device.arrived.

entries.summary: A registration was turned away.
entries.description: Carries the code, the connector and the fingerprint of a registration an operator refused. Every credential it held is forgotten with it, so a machine that was already approved stops being accepted on that connector's wire. It is not a permanent refusal: the machine registers again at its next boot and is given a new code, which announces itself here as any other code does.

entries.summary: A machine called a connector's wire and was turned away.
entries.description: Carries the connector, why the machine was refused, whether that connector asks a person to approve each machine or approves them on arrival, and the model and firmware the machine reported. The reason is unknown_credentials for credentials this server did not issue, and not_admitted for a machine the host would not take, such as one somebody retired. A refused machine usually calls again every few seconds, so the connector publishes at most one frame a minute for each machine, and a bounded number a minute in all. The machine's identity is never in the payload, only its SHA-256 digest, and neither is its network address.

entries.summary: An instruction was accepted for a device and is about to be sent.
entries.description: Carries the host-minted command_id, the verb, the caller's idempotency key, the capability epoch and digest the command was validated against, and the arguments as the caller sent them. It is the only one of the three command frames that carries a TTL, because it is the instruction and an instruction has a deadline. A consumer that acts on it checks the envelope's expiry first; a consumer that stores it does not. Arguments of a verb marked dangerous are published as their SHA-256 digest and never as text, and so are arguments that would break the 4 KiB bound on this payload. It carries no principal: who authorized the command is in com.prusa.connect.device.command.authorized alone.

entries.summary: An instruction ended, and this is what the host observed.
entries.description: Carries the command_id, the verb, how the command ended and how long it took. The status is one of succeeded, failed, refused, timed_out or abandoned, and a command whose caller went away while it may already have been on the wire is marked with the outcome unknown rather than guessed. It has no TTL, because the record of what happened never expires. It repeats none of the arguments: a consumer folds this frame together with the requested one by the causation id they share.

entries.summary: A principal authorized one instruction for a device.
entries.description: Carries the command_id, the verb and the authorizing principal as auth_type and auth_id, the same pair the envelope's audit attributes carry. The pair is in the payload as well as on the envelope because a store keeps the payload and not the envelope, and an audit record with no actor is not an audit record. Seeing it takes view_audit on the device, on the live stream and on the history read alike: viewing a printer is not being told which operator commanded it.

entries.summary: A camera produced a still image and the host stored it.
entries.description: Carries the camera, the printer it watches, the storage instance and the path the image was written to, its size in bytes and the moment the device produced the frame. It carries no image: a frame is megabytes and an event is a record of something happening, so what is here is where to fetch the picture from. It is published once per stored snapshot by the periodic capture an operator switches on per camera, and never by a snapshot somebody fetched over the API, because a read is not a thing that happened to the machine. It is a state event rather than telemetry, because a reader that missed one has a gap in the pictures of a print rather than a stale reading.

entries.summary: This host began moving a file from one of its storages onto a device.
entries.description: Carries the transfer_id, the storage and path the bytes come from, where the file lands on the device, and the file's length as the host measured it before the first byte left. The bytes move through this host: the device is never handed a URL to fetch, so this frame is the record that the file left a storage this deployment holds. It is a state event, because a reader that missed it holds a transfer it can never account for.

entries.summary: A transfer moved.
entries.description: Carries the transfer_id, the length, how many bytes this host has put on the wire and, for a device that reports one, how many the device says it has taken. It is telemetry: it is conflated on the way to a subscriber and it is not stored, because a record of every range of every file would grow with bytes moved rather than with things that happened. What a later reader gets is the started frame, the settled frame and the row folded from the two.

entries.summary: A transfer ended.
entries.description: Carries the transfer_id, how it ended, how many of how many bytes had left, why, and how long it ran. The state is one of done, failed, cancelled or interrupted. Interrupted is written on the next start for a transfer that was still running when this server stopped: it is not resumed, because the device has forgotten the transfer and the bytes it holds are a prefix nobody can name. A consumer folds this frame together with the started one by the transfer_id they share.

entries.summary: A print began on a device.
entries.description: Carries the job_id, the file on the machine and the name the machine shows for it, the instruction that started the print, and when this host first saw it. The command_id is absent for a print somebody started at the machine's own screen, because no instruction was sent. It names no person: who authorized the print is in com.prusa.connect.device.command.authorized, which takes view_audit, and the two are joined by the command_id. It fires once per print, on the first write of that print's row, so a host that restarts mid-print publishes nothing a second time. Progress is telemetry at /job/progress and is not here.

entries.summary: A print ended.
entries.description: Carries the job_id, the file, when the print ran, how it ended, the machine's own last word for it, the last progress reported, how long the machine says it printed and how much filament it says the print used. The outcome is one of finished, failed, cancelled and unknown, and it is the driver's reading of its machine's own word: a print that stopped without one is unknown, which is what a power cut looks like. The time printed and the filament used are absent for a machine that reports neither, and absent means unknown and never zero. It fires once per print, on the first reading that gives the print an end, so a machine that reports two terminal readings publishes one frame. A machine that loses its connection mid-print settles nothing: the print stays open and this frame follows when the machine comes back and says what happened.

entries.summary: A dashboard was made, changed or deleted.
entries.description: Carries the dashboard's id and the action: created, changed or deleted. The origin is the group of people who see it, dashboard:everyone, dashboard:operators or dashboard:admins, and a change that narrows who sees a dashboard is published to the group that saw it before. The frame carries no part of the dashboard: a screen drawing it reads it again, and one no longer allowed to see it is answered DASHBOARD_NOT_FOUND. Choosing the default publishes a change for the dashboard that stopped being it and for the one that became it.

entries.summary: The core upgrade transaction advanced.
entries.description: Carries the complete durable upgrade journal after a stage, verification, check, schedule or cancellation request. Its server origin is visible only to organization administrators. A reconnecting client reads the upgrade endpoint as its source of truth.
